title: 7.1-magnitude earthquake strikes southern Japan, tsunami alerts later lifted
dek: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture in southern Japan on Tuesday, triggering tsunami alerts for coastal regions that were subsequently lifted. No major damage, casualties, or nuclear plant abnormalities were reported, though authorities warned of possible aftershocks.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Japan Meteorological Agency registered the earthquake at 7.1 magnitude (U.S. Geological Survey recorded 6.8), centered near the city of Kumamoto about 600 miles south of Tokyo, per CBS News.
bottom_line: Initial reports show no major casualties or infrastructure damage, suggesting Japan's building standards and rapid warning systems functioned as designed. However, the government warned residents to prepare for aftershocks, and full damage assessments were still underway, meaning the picture could change as inspections of buildings and utilities proceed.
body: A powerful earthquake struck southern Japan on Tuesday, testing the country's disaster response systems and tsunami warning infrastructure. Japan Meteorological Agency registered the quake at magnitude 7.1, while the U.S. Geological Survey recorded 6.8, per CBS News. The earthquake was centered near the city of Kumamoto, about 600 miles south of Tokyo, in Kumamoto Prefecture.

Authorities issued a tsunami alert forecasting waves of about one yard in height, but lifted it after the initial assessment, according to CBS News reporting. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged residents to avoid coastlines due to the risk of possible tsunami waves and cautioned against complacency regarding possible strong aftershocks. The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center reported no tsunami threat to Hawaii or American Samoa.

The government response was rapid and precautionary. High-speed Shinkansen bullet trains and local trains in Kyushu were suspended temporarily for safety checks, per the reporting. The government established a task force to assess possible damage and prepare for any required rescue operations. Japan's Fire and Disaster Management Agency received no immediate reports of damage to major public facilities or infrastructure in the region, though assessments were still underway. No serious casualties or abnormalities at nuclear power plants in the region were reported.

The temblor measured at the highest possible level of seven on Japan's Shindo scale, the country's seismic intensity measurement system. The relatively modest damage reports reflect both the depth and distance of the epicenter and Japan's building codes and early warning systems, though full damage assessments continued hours after the quake struck.
